2 36 Rights to culture
3 Cultural rights—generally
4 (1) All persons with a particular cultural, religious, racial or linguistic
5 background must not be denied the right, in community with other
6 persons of that background, to enjoy their culture, to declare and
7 practise their religion and to use their language.
8 (2) All persons have the right:
9 (a) to take part in cultural life; and
10 (b) to enjoy the benefits of scientific progress and its
11 applications; and
12 (c) if a person is the author of any scientific, literary or artistic
13 production, to benefit from the protection of any moral and
14 material interests resulting from that production.
15 Note: In determining whether a limit on the right in subsection (2) is aimed
16 at achieving a legitimate objective (see paragraph 12(2)(b)), the
17 objective of promoting general welfare in a democratic society is
18 recognised under international human rights law as legitimate.
19 Cultural rights—Indigenous peoples
20 (3) Indigenous peoples hold distinct cultural rights.
21 (4) Indigenous peoples must not be denied the right, with other
22 members of their community:

24 and cultural heritage, including traditional knowledge,
25 distinctive spiritual practices, observances, beliefs and
26 teachings; and
27 (b) to enjoy, maintain, control, protect, develop and use their
28 languages, including traditional cultural expressions; and
29 (c) to enjoy, maintain, control, protect and develop their kinship
30 ties; and
31 (d) to maintain and strengthen distinctive spiritual, material and
32 economic relationship with the land, territories, waters,
33 coastal seas and other resources with which Indigenous

Part 3—Application of human rights
1
Division 1—Interpretation of laws
2
3 43 Interpretation
4 (1) A statutory provision must be interpreted, so far as is reasonably
5 possible, in a manner that is compatible with human rights.
6 (2) If a provision cannot be interpreted in a way that is compatible
7 with human rights, the provision must, to the extent possible that is
8 consistent with its purpose, be interpreted in a way that is most
9 compatible with human rights.
10 (3) International human rights law and the judgments of domestic,
11 foreign and international courts and tribunals relevant to a human
12 right may be considered in interpreting a statutory provision.
13 Note: International human rights law is defined in section 6.
14 (4) This section does not affect the validity of:
15 (a) an Act or provision of an Act that is not compatible with
16 human rights; or
17 (b) a legislative instrument or a provision of a legislative
18 instrument that is not compatible with human rights and is
19 expressly empowered by the Act under which it is made to
20 not be compatible with human rights.
21 44 Intervention by Attorney-General
22 (1) The Attorney-General may intervene in, and may be joined as a
23 party to, any proceeding before a court in which:
24 (a) a question of law arises that relates to the application of this
25 Act; or
26 (b) a question arises in relation to the interpretation of a statutory
27 provision in accordance with this Act.
28 (2) If the Attorney-General intervenes in a proceeding under this
29 section, the Attorney-General may be taken to be a party to the
30 proceeding for the purpose of any appeal from an order made in
31 that proceeding.

Division 2—Public authorities
1
2 47 Obligations on public authorities
3 (1) It is unlawful for a public authority:
4 (a) to act or make a decision in a way that is not compatible with
5 human rights; or
6 (b) in making a decision, to fail to give proper consideration to a
7 human right relevant to the decision.
8 (2) Subsection (1) does not apply to a public authority if the authority
9 could not reasonably have acted differently or made a different
10 decision because of a statutory provision, a law of a State or
11 Territory or otherwise under law.
12 Example: Where a public authority is acting to give effect to an Act or
13 legislative instrument that is not compatible with human rights.
14 (3) This section does not apply to an act or decision of a private nature.
15 (4) For subsection (1)(b), giving proper consideration to a human right
16 in making a decision includes, but is not limited to:
17 (a) identifying the human rights that may be affected by the
18 decision; and
19 (b) considering whether the decision would be compatible with
20 human rights; and
21 (c) ensuring the participation of:
22 (i) Indigenous peoples in decisions that directly or
23 disproportionately affect Indigenous peoples;
24 (ii) children in decisions that directly or disproportionately
25 affect children;
26 (iii) people with disability in decisions that directly or
27 disproportionately affect people with disability; and
28 (d) where relevant, realising access to justice principles.
29 (5) To avoid doubt:
30 (a) an act or decision of a public authority is not invalid merely
31 because, by doing the act or making the decision, the
32 authority contravenes subsection (1); and
